title: The Assembled Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Text and Phrase)
excerpt: Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Grdhrakuta in Rajagriha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand monks.

inline.s: Upholding
the precepts and scripture, as a pauper who has found a treasure.

rows.s: Chapter Forty-Five: This Scripture Alone Shall Remain
Chapter Forty-Seven: Merit and Wisdom First Hear It
Chapter Forty-Four: Receiving the Prophecy of Bodhi
Chapter Forty-Six: Practice Diligently and Hold Firmly
Chapter Forty-Eight: The Benefits of Hearing This Sutra

inline.s: Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Grdhrakuta in Rajagriha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand monks.

All these great sages, whose spiritual powers had already been attained, their names being: the Venerable Ajnata Kaundinya, the Venerable Right Vow, the Venerable Right Speech, the Venerable Great Cry, the Venerable Amiable and Wise, the Venerable Free from Defilement, the Venerable Well-Known, the Venerable Truly Attained, the Venerable Complete, the Venerable Ox-King, the Venerable Uruvilva Kasyapa, the Venerable Gaya Kasyapa, the Venerable Nadi Kasyapa, the Venerable Mahakasyapa, the Venerable Sariputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the Venerable Kalpina, the Venerable Great Abiding, the Venerable Great Pure Resolve, the Venerable Mahacunda, the Venerable Full Vow, the Venerable Free of Obstacles, the Venerable Flowing Pour, the Venerable Firm and Subduing, the Venerable King of Forms, the Venerable Vehicle of Fruition, the Venerable Benevolent Nature, the Venerable Joyful, the Venerable Welcome, the Venerable Rahula, the Venerable Ananda
and others, who were at the head of the assembly.
There were also the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Manjusri, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and all the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, who all came together to the gathering.

blocks.text: Chapter Two: Accordance with the Virtue of Samantabhadra

inline.s: There were also sixteen noble ones, namely the Bodhisattva Bhadrapala, the Bodhisattva of Good Reflection, the Bodhisattva of Wisdom and Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Who Contemplates Non-abiding, the Bodhisattva of Supernatural Flower, the Bodhisattva of Radiant Splendor, the Bodhisattva of the Jeweled Banner, the Bodhisattva of Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva of Tranquil Faculties, the Bodhisattva of Faith and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva of Vow and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva of the Fragrant Elephant, the Bodhisattva of the Jeweled Flower, the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Middle, the Bodhisattva of Controlling Conduct, and the Bodhisattva of Liberation, who were at their head.

They all together reverently practiced the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra, were complete in immeasurable practices and vows, and abode in the Dharma of merit and virtue. They roamed the ten directions with expedient means, entered the treasury of the Buddha Dharma, and reached the ultimate other shore.

Having vowed to attain perfect enlightenment in immeasurable worlds, they left the Tushita Heaven, renounced the throne, went forth from home, and practiced austerities in the pursuit of the Way. These manifestations they made out of conformity with the world. By meditation and wisdom they subdued the maras and their hosts, attained the subtle Dharma, and realized perfect enlightenment.

Gods and humans turned to them in reverence and entreated them to turn the wheel of the Dharma. With the sound of the Dharma they awakened the world, broke through the citadel of afflictions, destroyed the moat of desires, washed away all defilement, and revealed purity. They harmonized beings, proclaimed the wondrous principle, stored up merit, and showed the field of merit. With the medicine of the Dharma they cured the threefold suffering. They ascended to the stage of consecration and bestowed the prophecy of bodhi. To teach the bodhisattvas they served as acaryas, practicing the boundless, corresponding practices, maturing the boundless roots of good of the bodhisattvas, and immeasurable Buddhas together protected and remembered them.

In the Buddha lands they all could manifest themselves. Like a skilled magician who displays various different forms, yet in those forms there is nothing to be grasped: these bodhisattvas are likewise. They penetrate the nature of all dharmas and understand the characteristics of sentient beings. They make offerings to the Buddhas and open the way for sentient beings. They manifest their bodies like a flash of lightning, tearing apart the net of maras' false views and releasing all the bonds. They lead beings far beyond the stage of the hearers and the pratyekabuddhas, and enter the Dharma gate of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Skillfully establishing expedient means, they reveal the three vehicles.

Among those of inferior and middling capacity they manifest nirvana. They attain the samadhis of non-arising and non-ceasing, and all the doors of dharani. At all times they awaken to and enter the Avatamsaka samadhi, endowed with hundreds and thousands of samadhis. Dwelling in deep meditation, they see all the immeasurable Buddhas, and in a single thought they travel throughout all Buddha lands.

The great beings appear, attain the Buddha's eloquence, and abide in the practice of Samantabhadra. Skillfully they distinguish the languages of sentient beings, and reveal the reality of the ultimate, surpassing all the dharmas of the world. Their minds constantly abide in the Way that saves the world; toward all things they are free and at ease, and they are friends who go uninvited to the aid of all kinds of beings. They uphold the Thus-Come One's profound treasury of Dharma and guard the Buddha's seed of enlightenment so that it never ceases.

They arouse great compassion, pity sentient beings, proclaim compassionate eloquence, bestow the Dharma-eye, close the evil destinies, and open the door of goodness. Toward all beings they regard them as themselves, rescuing and bearing them up, and deliver them all to the other shore. They fully obtain the immeasurable virtues of the Buddhas, with wisdom and sagely brightness beyond thought.

All such great bodhisattvas, immeasurable and boundless, came together at that time. There were also five hundred bhikshunis, seven thousand upasakas, five hundred upasikas, and the gods of the realm of desire and the realm of form, with all the heavenly brahma multitudes, present at the great assembly.

blocks.text: Chapter Three: The Occasion of the Great Teaching

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One's majestic radiance shone brightly, like a mass of molten gold, and again like a bright mirror, its glow penetrating within and without, manifesting a great light with hundreds and thousands of transformations. The Venerable Ananda then reflected: Today the World-Honored One's bodily form and his faculties are joyous and pure, his radiant countenance towering, and this precious land is adorned, such as has never been seen from the beginning. I rejoice to gaze upon it and have given rise to a mind of wonder.

He then rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his knees on the ground, and with palms together said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, today you have entered the great still samadhi, abiding in the extraordinary Dharma, abiding in the practice of the guide and teacher in which all Buddhas abide, the supreme Way. Past, future, and present, Buddha after Buddha think of one another. Do you think of the Buddhas of the past and the future? Or do you think of the Buddhas now in other directions? Why is your majestic power so brilliant, your auspicious rays so surpassingly wondrous? We beseech you to proclaim it.

Then the World-Honored One said to Ananda: Excellent! Excellent! For pitying and benefiting sentient beings, you are able to ask this subtle meaning. This question of yours surpasses making offerings to all the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of a single world, and surpasses giving to gods and humans of many aeons, beings such as winged
xuan
flitting and wriggling
(ru)
creatures, by hundreds of thousands of times. Why? Because the gods and humans of ages to come, and all that live, will, because of your asking, be delivered.
Ananda, the Thus-Come One, with his inexhaustible great compassion, feels pity
jin

for the three realms, and therefore has appeared in the world. He proclaims the Way of the Dharma, wishing to rescue the masses of beings and bestow upon them the real benefit. Hard to meet, hard to see, like the udumbara flower, he rarely appears in the world. What you have now asked brings much benefit to beings.

Ananda, you should know that the Thus-Come One's perfect enlightenment and his wisdom are hard to measure and are without obstruction. In a single thought he can abide through immeasurable millions of aeons, yet his body and faculties are without increase or decrease. Why is this? Because his meditation and wisdom are completely pervading and without limit; therefore in all dharmas he attains the supreme freedom.
Ananda, listen attentively and think well upon it; I shall explain it to you in detail.

The Buddha told Ananda: In the past, long ago, in immeasurable, inconceivable, incalculable aeons, the Thus-Come One Radiant Glow appeared in the world, taught and delivered immeasurable sentient beings, and caused them all to attain the Way, and then entered nirvana. Next came a Thus-Come One named Far-Reaching Light, then Moonlight, then Sandalwood Fragrance, then King of Good Mountains, then Sumeru Heavenly Crown, then Sumeru Equaling Light, then Moon-Radiance, then Right Mindfulness, then Free of Defilement, then Non-attached, then Dragon and Heaven, then Night Light, then Peak of Bright Serenity, then Unmoving Ground, then Wondrous Flower of Lapis Lazuli, then Golden Color of Lapis Lazuli, then Gold Treasury, then Blazing Light, then Blazing Root, then Earth Seed, then Moon Image, then Sun Sound, then Flower of Liberation, then Adorned Light, then Ocean Awakening Supernatural Power, then Water Light, then Great Fragrance, then Free of Dust and Defilement, then Renouncing Discontent, then Jewel Blaze, then Wondrous Peak, then Brave Standing, then Merit-Upholding Wisdom, then Shading Sun and Moon Light, then Sun-Moon Lapis Light, then Supreme Lapis Light, then Foremost, then Flower of Bodhi, then Bright Moon, then Sunlight, then King of Flower-Colors, then Water-Moon Light, then Dispelling Delusion's Darkness, then Practice Surmounting the Hindrances, then Pure Faith, then Good Dwelling, then Awesome Power, then Dharma Wisdom, then Phoenix Sound, then Lion Sound, then Dragon Sound, then Abiding in the World. All such Buddhas have indeed already passed away.
At that time, next there was a Buddha

named Lokesvararaja, the Thus-Come One, the Worthy of Offerings, the one fully and rightly Enlightened, the one Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Supreme Guide, the Tamer of Persons, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. In the world he taught for forty-two aeons, and at that time, for the gods and the people of the world, he expounded the scriptures and preached the Way.

There was a great king named World-Abundant King who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, rejoiced and gained understanding, and at once brought forth the aspiration for the supreme, true Way. He abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship, became a wandering monk, and took the name Dharmakara, practicing the bodhisattva's path.

Of lofty talent, brave and wise, he was unsurpassed in the world; in faith, understanding, and clear memory he was foremost in all things. He had supreme practices and vows, and the power of mindfulness and wisdom, which strengthened his mind, firm and unmovable. In practice he was so diligent that none could surpass him.
Repairing to the place of the Buddha, he bowed his head at his feet and knelt, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, he praised him in gatha verses and set forth vast vows.
The verses say:
The Thus-Come One's subtle, majestic form, all things in the world have nothing to equal it,
His immeasurable light illumines the ten directions; sun, moon, and fire-jewels all hide their radiance.
The World-Honored One can voice a single sound, and beings each understand it according to their kind,
He can also manifest a single wondrous body, universally causing sentient beings to see it according to their kind.
May I attain the Buddha's pure voice, the sound of the Dharma spreading throughout all bounds,
Proclaiming the gates of precepts, meditation, and diligence, and penetrating the profound, subtle Dharma.
His wisdom is vast and deep as the sea, his inner mind pure, cut off from worldly toil,
Surpassing the gates of the boundless evil destinies, speedily reaching the ultimate shore of bodhi.
Ignorance, greed, and anger all forever gone, delusion ended and faults extinguished by the power of samadhi,
Like the immeasurable Buddhas of the past, a great guide for the multitudes of beings.
Able to save all the worlds and their beings from birth, aging, illness, and death, and their many sufferings,
Always practicing giving, precepts, and patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom, the six perfections.
The not-yet-delivered beings he causes to be delivered; those already delivered he causes to become Buddhas,
Even offering to sages numerous as the sands of the Ganges is not equal to firmly and bravely seeking enlightenment.
May I abide in samadhi, always emitting light to illumine all,
And, because of this, obtain a vast, pure abode, supremely adorned beyond all compare.
Beings wandering through the realms of samsara, may they quickly be born in my land and receive peace and happiness,
Ever setting compassion to work to rescue beings, delivering all the boundless suffering creatures.
My practice is that of the power of firm resolve; only the Buddha's sagely wisdom can know and attest it,
Even though my body dwell in the midst of all suffering, this vow and heart shall never retreat.

blocks.text: Chapter Five: The Selection of the Buddha Land

inline.s: The monk Dharmakara, having spoken these verses, said to the Buddha: Now, for the bodhisattva path, I have brought forth the aspiration for supreme enlightenment, and undertake the vow to become a Buddha, causing all beings to be as the Buddha. I beseech the Buddha to proclaim the scriptures and Dharma widely; I shall uphold them and practice as taught, cutting off the root of all the toil of birth and death, and speedily attain the supreme, perfect enlightenment.

When I become a Buddha, may my wisdom, my light, the land where I dwell, and the name of its teacher all be heard throughout the ten directions. May the gods and humans, and the flitting, wriggling creatures that come to be born in my land, all become bodhisattvas. I set this vow, that it should surpass countless Buddha lands in every way; is this attainable?

The Buddha Lokesvararaja then spoke to Dharmakara, saying: For example, the great ocean, though one man might measure it with a bushel through age after age, could yet reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous jewels. If a person seeks the Way with utmost sincerity and is unceasingly diligent, he will certainly accomplish the fruit; what vow could he not fulfill?

You should consider for yourself: what expedient means, once cultivated, can accomplish the adornment of a Buddha land? As is your practice, so you yourself should know. The pure Buddha land you should yourself take up and perfect.

Dharmakara replied: This meaning is vast and profound, beyond my sphere. I only beseech the Thus-Come One, the Worthy of Offerings, the fully and rightly Enlightened, to proclaim widely the immeasurable wondrous lands of the Buddhas. If I hear such dharmas, and reflect upon and practice them, I vow to fulfill all my wishes.

The Buddha Lokesvararaja, knowing his loftiness and wisdom and the depth and breadth of his vows, proclaimed for him the Buddha lands of two hundred and ten kotis, with their merit, adornment, and purity, and their vast, complete, and perfect characteristics. In accord with his wish, he revealed them all to him. When this Dharma was spoken, a thousand koti ages passed.

At that time Dharmakara, hearing what the Buddha had spoken and seeing it all, brought forth the supreme and unsurpassed vow. Regarding the good and evil of the gods and humans there, and the coarse and fine of those lands, he reflected upon them to the ultimate. Then with single mind he selected what he desired and formed his great vows.

He sought with vigor and diligence, kept with reverence and care, and practiced merit and virtue for five aeons. Regarding the merit and adornment of all those two hundred and ten koti Buddha lands, he understood and penetrated them clearly, as if they were a single Buddha land. The Buddha land he thereby selected surpassed them all.

Having made his selection, he again went to the Thus-Come One Lokesvararaja. Bowing his head at his feet, he circumambulated the Buddha three times, and standing with palms together, said to the World-Honored One: I have now accomplished the pure practice of the selection of the Buddha land.

The Buddha said: Excellent! Now is the very time; you should fully proclaim it, causing the assembly to rejoice. Let this great multitude, upon hearing this Dharma, obtain great good and benefit, and be able to practice the selection in the Buddha land and fulfill immeasurable great vows.
Dharmakara said: I only beseech the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, to hear and consider me.
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, there are in my land hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 01: No Evil Destinies)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, after their lives end the gods and humans of my land should fall again into the three evil destinies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 02: No Falling Again into the Evil Destinies)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not all have bodies of the true golden color, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 03: Bodies of True Gold)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should differ in form and color, there being fair and ugly ones, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 04: Neither Fair nor Ugly)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not have the super-knowledge of past lives, at the least to know the matters of hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of aeons, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 05: Knowledge of Past Lives)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not have the divine eye, at the least to see the Buddha lands of hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 06: The Divine Eye)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not have the divine ear, at the least to hear what is spoken by hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of Buddhas, and not fully uphold it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 07: The Divine Ear)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not have the knowledge of the minds of others, at the least to know the thoughts of the beings in the Buddha lands of hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 08: Reading the Minds of Others)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not have the super-knowledge of spiritual powers, at the least unable in a single thought to pass beyond the Buddha lands of hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 09: Unobstructed Spiritual Powers)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should give rise to thoughts that cling to and reckon upon the body, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 10: No Clinging to the Body)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not abide in the correct and certain destiny, surely to reach nirvana, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 11: Abiding in the Correct Destiny)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, my light should be limited, at the least not illumining the Buddha lands of hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 12: Immeasurable Light)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, my life-span should be limited, at the least to hundreds of thousands of kotis of nayutas of aeons, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 13: Immeasurable Life)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hearers in my land are countless; even if all the beings in the three thousand great thousand worlds were to become pratyekabuddhas and, united, were to count them for hundreds of thousands of aeons and could ascertain their number, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 14: Countless Hearers)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should have immeasurable life-span, except that as their original vows may be, their length and shortness of life are at freedom. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 15: Immeasurable Lifespan)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should hear even the name of anything unwholesome, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 16: Hearing No Unwholesome Names)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions should not all praise and invoke my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 17: Praise by All the Buddhas)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere mind and joyous faith, aspire to be born in my land and call upon me even ten times; if they should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Only excluding those who commit the five gravest offenses and slander the true Dharma.
(Vow 18: Birth Attained by Ten Calls)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, having brought forth the bodhi mind, practice various merits and with sincere mind make the vow to be born in my land, and at the end of their lives, if I should not appear before them surrounded by the great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 19: Birth by a Sincere Mind)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, hearing my name, fix their thoughts on my land, plant various roots of virtue, and with sincere mind dedicate the merit, aspiring to be born in my land; if they should not accomplish it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 20: Dedication of Merit for Birth)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not all have the thirty-two marks of the great man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 21: The Thirty-Two Marks)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the Buddha lands in other directions who come to be born in my land shall ultimately and surely reach the stage of one lifetime before Buddhahood. Except those who, in accordance with their original vows, for the sake of beings, don the armor of the great vow and enter the worlds of other directions to deliver all beings at will. Wandering through the Buddha lands, practicing the bodhisattva's course, accumulating roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Thus-Come Ones of the ten directions, they teach and transform sentient beings numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to stand on the supreme, true Way, surpassing the ordinary stages of practice, and now manifestly practicing the virtue of Samantabhadra. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 22: Reaching the Stage of One Lifetime)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, by the Buddha's spiritual power, make offerings to the Buddhas, yet in the space of a single meal cannot go everywhere throughout the immeasurable, countless kotis of nayutas of Buddha lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 23: Making Offerings to All the Buddhas)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, when before the Buddhas, should not have the offerings they require at their will, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 24: Offerings at Will)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not be able to expound the all-knowing wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 25: Expounding the Wondrous Wisdom)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not obtain the adamantine body of narayana, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 26: The Narayana Body)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, all the things in my land, for both the gods and humans, are adorned, pure, radiant, and beautiful, with forms and colors extraordinary and exquisite beyond all description; if the beings there, even having obtained the divine eye, could clearly distinguish and name their numbers, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 27: All Adorned and Pure)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, even those with only slight merit, should not be able to know and see the immeasurable light and color of the bodhi-tree of the enlightenment ground, which is four million li high, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 28: Seeing the Bodhi Tree)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, if they receive and read the scriptures, chant, uphold, and expound them, should not attain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 29: Wisdom from Chanting the Sutras)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land could be measured or limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 30: Unbounded Wisdom and Eloquence)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, my land is pure and the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha worlds of the ten directions are all clearly reflected in it, as in a bright mirror one sees one's own image and face. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 31: Reflecting All the Ten Directions)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, from the ground up to the sky, the palaces, towers, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, and all things in my land, are all made by the intermingling of immeasurable jewels and fragrances, adorned in wonderful array surpassing the gods and humans, and their fragrance pervades all the worlds of the ten directions; and if the bodhisattvas who smell it do not all practice the Buddha's way, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 32: The Wondrous Adornment of Jewel and Fragrance)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha worlds of the ten directions, whose bodies are touched by my light, become pliant in body and mind, surpassing the gods and humans. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 33: Pliant Through Touching My Light)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, should not attain the bodhisattva's patience of non-arising and the deep dharani, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 34: Attaining Patience by Hearing the Name)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, may there be no women in my land. Women who wish to be born in my land shall be transformed into men. The countless gods and humans, even down to the flitting, wriggling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotus flowers upon the seven-juweled ponds, and when grown up, are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 35: No Women, Birth by Lotus)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, after the end of their lives, always practice the pure course until they attain the Buddha Way. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 36: The Pure Life Ever Practiced)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, prostrate themselves with all five members of the body, bow their heads in homage, rejoice, believe, and take joy, and practice the bodhisattva's course; and if the gods and humans of all worlds do not reverence them, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 37: Revering the Gods and Humans)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land, desiring clothing, should have it come to them at their thought, and, as the Buddha praises, the wonderful robes in accord with the Dharma should naturally appear on their bodies. If they should have to cut, sew, dye, or wash them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 38: Clothing at Will)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the happiness enjoyed by the gods and humans in my land should not be like that of the monks whose outflows are exhausted, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 39: Joy Like the Outflowless)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, wishing at will to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure Buddha lands of the ten directions, should, at that very time and according to their wishes, see them all clearly reflected in the jewel-trees, as in a bright mirror one beholds one's own face. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 40: Buddha Lands Reflected in the Trees)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, until they attain Buddhahood, should have their faculties imperfect or deficient, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 41: Perfect Faculties)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, all attain the samadhi of pure liberation. Abiding in this samadhi, in a single moment of thought, they make offerings to the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, without losing their concentration. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 42: Offering While in Samadhi)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, after the end of their lives, should be born into a noble and honored family. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 43: Noble Birth by Hearing the Name)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, rejoice and leap with joy, practice the bodhisattva's course, and are complete in the roots of virtue. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 44: Fulness of the Roots of Virtue)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, all attain the universal samadhi. Abiding in this samadhi, until they become Buddhas, they are always facing the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 45: The Universal Samadhi)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their vows, whatever Dharma they wish to hear, all hear it of themselves. If it be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 46: Hearing the Dharma According to Wishes)
If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, should not at once attain non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 47: Non-retrogression by Hearing the Name)

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the hosts of bodhisattvas of the lands in other directions, hearing my name, should not at once attain the first, second, and third patiences of the Dharma, and should not at once attain non-retrogression in the Dharma of all the Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(Vow 48: Attaining the Three Patiences of the Dharma)

blocks.text: Chapter Seven: The Certain Attainment of Enlightenment

inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: At that time, the monk Dharmakara, having spoken these vows, praised him in verses, saying:
I have set a resolve surpassing the world, surely to attain the supreme Way; if this vow be not fulfilled, I swear never to attain perfect enlightenment.
Again I have become a great giver, universally aiding all the poor and suffering, causing the multitudes of beings throughout the long night of being to have no grief or distress.
Bringing forth all roots of goodness, and accomplishing the fruit of bodhi; when I attain perfect enlightenment, I shall be named Immeasurable Life.
All beings who hear this name shall come to my land; like the Buddha's golden body, their wondrous marks all complete.
With the great compassionate heart, I will benefit all beings; freeing them from desire, deep in right mindfulness, I will practice the pure life with pure wisdom.
May my wisdom-light universally illumine the lands of the ten directions, clearing away the darkness of the three poisons, and brightly delivering beings from all their perils and calamities.
May all beings renounce the suffering of the three evil paths, extinguish the darkness of afflictions, open the eye of wisdom, and obtain the body of light.
Sealing all the evil destinies, and opening wide the door of the good course; for beings I will open the treasury of the Dharma and broadly bestow the jewels of merit and virtue.
With the unhindered wisdom of the Buddha, practicing the compassionate acts, always a teacher of gods and humans, becoming a hero of the three realms.
Preaching the Dharma with the lion's roar, broadly delivering all beings, fulfilling the vows of former times, and causing all things to become Buddhas.
If this vow be accomplished, the great thousand worlds should tremble with emotion, and the gods and spirits in the sky shall rain down precious, wondrous flowers.

The Buddha told Ananda: When the monk Dharmakara had spoken these verses, at once the whole earth quaked in six ways. The heavens rained wonderful flowers, scattering them upon him. Natural music arose, and from the sky a voice of praise declared: He will surely attain the supreme perfect enlightenment.

blocks.text: Chapter Eight: The Accumulation of Merit and Virtue

inline.s: Ananda, the monk Dharmakara, having set forth this great vow before the Thus-Come One Lokesvararaja and in the midst of the assembly of gods and humans, abode in the true wisdom, and was brave and diligent, single-mindedly devoted to adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha land he cultivated was vast and spacious, unsurpassed and uniquely wondrous, established to endure for all time, without decay and without change.

Throughout immeasurable aeons he accumulated and planted virtue and conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire, and was not attached to form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. He delighted only in recollecting the roots of good cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the practice of stillness, far from all falsehood. Relying on the gate of the true meaning, he planted the roots of all virtues, not counting the many hardships.

He was of few desires and knew contentment, single-mindedly seeking the wholesome Dharma, benefiting and aiding all beings. In his vows and aspirations he never tired, and the power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he constantly harbored compassion and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them onward. He revered the Three Jewels and served his teachers and elders, without any false or flattering heart.
